steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a survey paper on fairness testing of machine learning software, from a software engineering perspective. It should motivate why fairness matters, define the problem and its challenges, explain what the survey covers and how it differs from earlier surveys, and list the contributions.

- History of fairness research
- Fairness as a software engineering concern
- Fairness bugs and fairness testing; challenges vs traditional testing
- Growth of the field and scope of this survey
- Comparison with previous surveys
- Contributions and paper structure

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Machine Learning (ML)-enabled software, which is often called ML software, is now widely used in critical areas of society, such as hiring, credit assessment, and criminal justice. But using this software has also caused cases of unfair decision-making, especially when sensitive attributes like sex, race, age, and occupation are involved. For example, an ML-enabled recidivism assessment system used by US courts was found to wrongly label black defendants as higher-risk than white defendants.

These unfair behaviors of ML software can have serious ethical implications and lead to unacceptable outcomes, especially by disadvantaging minority groups and protected categories. Because of this, the research community is more and more concerned and aware about unfairness and its impact.

Research on fairness issues really gained momentum in the late 1960s, when psychometricians started to investigate whether educational tests were fair. In the 1980s, researchers looked into the social impact of technology. After that, starting around 2008, the study of fairness expanded to ML and Software Engineering (SE), because ML was quickly adopted in software applications that support decision-making.

From the SE perspective, fairness is a non-functional software property and it should be treated as a first-class entity in the whole SE process. Ahmad et al. said that fairness is becoming more important as a requirement that has to be considered in the requirements engineering phase of ML software development. Alidoosti argued that fairness should be included in the design process of software architecture. Albarghouthi et al. framed fairness as correctness properties for verifying ML programs. Zhang et al. described fairness as an important testing property for ML software. Also, Zhang et al. saw fairness as the objective of repairing ML software.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Machine Learning (ML)-enabled software, which is often called ML software, is now widely used in critical areas of society, such as hiring, credit assessment, and criminal justice. But using this software has also caused cases of unfair decision-making, especially when sensitive attributes like sex, race, age, and occupation are involved. For example, an ML-enabled recidivism assessment system used by US courts was found to wrongly label black defendants as higher-risk than white defendants.

These unfair behaviors of ML software can have serious ethical implications and lead to unacceptable outcomes, especially by disadvantaging minority groups and protected categories. Because of this, the research community is more and more concerned and aware about unfairness and its impact.

Research on fairness issues really gained momentum in the late 1960s, when psychometricians started to investigate whether educational tests were fair. In the 1980s, researchers looked into the social impact of technology. After that, starting around 2008, the study of fairness expanded to ML and Software Engineering (SE), because ML was quickly adopted in software applications that support decision-making.

From the SE perspective, fairness is a non-functional software property and it should be treated as a first-class entity in the whole SE process. Ahmad et al. said that fairness is becoming more important as a requirement that has to be considered in the requirements engineering phase of ML software development. Alidoosti argued that fairness should be included in the design process of software architecture. Albarghouthi et al. framed fairness as correctness properties for verifying ML programs. Zhang et al. described fairness as an important testing property for ML software. Also, Zhang et al. saw fairness as the objective of repairing ML software.

In this paper we also look at fairness from the SE perspective. We define fairness bugs as imperfections in software systems that cause a misalignment between the desired fairness conditions and the actual outcomes. We focus on fairness testing of ML software, which tries to uncover fairness bugs by executing code. Fairness testing is an important part of software fairness research and it is closely connected to other activities in the SE process. It checks whether software systems meet fairness requirements, it exposes fairness bugs that were introduced during implementation, and it guides software repair to address fairness issues, among other SE activities.

Fairness testing has different challenges than traditional software testing. For example, in traditional software testing a test oracle usually relies on the output of a single input. In fairness testing the oracle problem is harder because inputs and outputs from different demographic groups have to be considered at the same time. Also, there are many different fairness definitions, and some of them even conflict with each other or are mathematically impossible to satisfy at the same time. Different definitions can need different test oracles, so designing fairness testing techniques that handle all these definitions is a big problem too.

Because fairness testing is important and has these challenges, research in this field has increased a lot. Figure 1 shows the cumulative number of publications on fairness testing until 2023, which shows growing interest and why this survey is relevant. 89% of fairness testing publications have appeared since 2019, which shows that this is a new emerging domain of software testing.

This paper gives a comprehensive survey of fairness testing in ML software. The papers we collected come from different venues, including SE, artificial intelligence, computer security, and human-computer interaction. We categorize them by two key aspects: the fairness testing workflow (i.e., how to test) and the fairness testing components (i.e., what to test). We also analyze research trends and identify research opportunities for the fairness testing community. We also give an overview of public datasets and open-source tools for fairness testing.

There have been previous surveys on different aspects of fairness in ML and related fields. Mehrabi et al. and Pessach and Shmueli surveyed fairness research on ML algorithms, and Hort et al. focused on bias mitigation methods for ML classifiers. Sun et al., Berk et al., and Pitoura et al. surveyed techniques for improving fairness in specific ML tasks, like natural language processing, criminal justice risk assessment, and ranking. Tushev et al. surveyed software design strategies for fairness in digital sharing economy applications. Hutchinson and Mitchell gave a historical perspective on fairness assessment tests in different disciplines, including education and hiring. Zhang et al. did a broader survey on ML testing where fairness is one of several testing properties. A recent systematic literature review was about software fairness but covered only 20 fairness testing papers. Our survey instead concentrates specifically on fairness testing of ML software. As far as we know, this is the first comprehensive survey dedicated to the fairness testing literature.

In summary, the contributions of this work are:

- • A comprehensive survey of 100 fairness testing papers from different research communities.

- • A definition of fairness bug and fairness testing, and an overview of the testing workflow and testing components in fairness testing.

- • A summary of public datasets and open-source tools for fairness testing, as a navigation for researchers and practitioners interested in the field.

- • An analysis of research trends and promising research opportunities in fairness testing, to help further advances in this area.

Figure 2 shows the structure of the paper, and Section 3 presents the detailed survey methodology.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Machine Learning (ML)-enabled software, commonly referred to as ML software, has been widely adopted in critical areas of society, including hiring [1], credit assessment [2], and criminal justice [3]. However, the use of such software has also led to instances of unfair decision-making, particularly when sensitive attributes such as sex, race, age, and occupation are involved [4]. For instance, an ML-enabled recidivism assessment system used by US courts was found to incorrectly label black defendants as higher-risk individuals compared to white defendants [5].

The unfair behaviors of ML software can have profound ethical implications, resulting in unacceptable outcomes, particularly by disadvantaging minority groups and protected categories. Consequently, there is growing concern and awareness within the research community about the issue of unfairness and its impact.

The exploration of fairness issues gained significant momentum in the late 1960s [6], when psychometricians began investigating the fairness of educational tests [7,8]. In the 1980s, researchers turned to the social impact of technology [9]. Subsequently, beginning around 2008, the study of fairness expanded to the domains of ML [10] and Software Engineering (SE) [11], in response to the rapid adoption of ML in software applications that support decision-making.

From the SE perspective, fairness is a non-functional software property that should be treated as a first-class entity throughout the SE process [4,12]. Ahmad et al. [13] emphasized the growing importance of fairness as a requirement to be considered during the requirements engineering phase of ML software development. Alidoosti [14] argued for including fairness considerations in the design process of software architecture. Albarghouthi et al. [15] framed fairness as correctness properties for ML program verification. Zhang et al. [16] described fairness as a significant testing property for ML software. Additionally, Zhang et al. [17] viewed fairness as the objective of repairing ML software.

In this paper, we also approach fairness from the SE perspective and define as fairness bugs those imperfections in software systems that result in a misalignment between desired fairness conditions and actual outcomes. We focus on fairness testing of ML software, which aims to uncover fairness bugs through code execution. Fairness testing is an important aspect of software fairness research and is closely intertwined with other activities in the SE process. It verifies whether software systems meet fairness requirements, exposes fairness bugs introduced during implementation, and guides software repair efforts to address fairness issues, among other SE activities.

Compared to traditional software testing, fairness testing presents distinct challenges. For example, in traditional software testing, a test oracle typically relies on the output of a single input. In fairness testing, the oracle problem is harder because inputs and outputs from different demographic groups must be considered simultaneously. In addition, there are diverse fairness definitions, some of which may conflict with each other or be mathematically impossible to satisfy concurrently [18,19]. Since different definitions can require different test oracles, designing fairness testing techniques that accommodate this multitude of definitions is a significant problem as well.

The importance of fairness testing and its challenges have led to a notable increase in research effort in this field. Figure 1 shows the cumulative number of publications on fairness testing until 2023, revealing a growing interest and underlining the relevance of this survey. Notably, 89% of fairness testing publications have appeared since 2019, indicating the emergence of this new domain of software testing.

This paper offers a comprehensive survey of fairness testing in ML software. The collected papers come from various venues including SE, artificial intelligence, computer security, and human-computer interaction. We categorize these papers along two key aspects: the fairness testing workflow (i.e., how to test) and fairness testing components (i.e., what to test). Furthermore, we analyze research trends and identify potential research opportunities for the fairness testing community. We also provide an overview of publicly accessible datasets and open-source tools for fairness testing.

Previous surveys have explored various aspects of fairness in ML and related fields. Mehrabi et al. [20] and Pessach and Shmueli [21] surveyed fairness research on ML algorithms, while Hort et al. [22] focused on bias mitigation methods for ML classifiers. Sun et al. [23], Berk et al. [3], and Pitoura et al. [24] surveyed techniques for improving fairness in specific ML tasks, such as natural language processing, criminal justice risk assessment, and ranking. Tushev et al. [25] surveyed software design strategies for fairness in digital sharing economy applications. Hutchinson and Mitchell [6] gave a historical perspective on fairness assessment tests across disciplines, including education and hiring. Zhang et al. [16] conducted a broader survey on ML testing, treating fairness as one of several testing properties. A recent systematic literature review [26] focused on software fairness but covered only 20 fairness testing papers. In contrast, our survey concentrates specifically on fairness testing of ML software. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive survey dedicated to the fairness testing literature.

To summarize, this work makes the following contributions:

- • It provides a comprehensive survey of 100 fairness testing papers from diverse research communities.

- • It defines fairness bug and fairness testing, and gives an overview of the testing workflow and testing components of fairness testing.

- • It summarizes public datasets and open-source tools for fairness testing, providing navigation for researchers and practitioners interested in the field.

- • It analyzes research trends and identifies promising research opportunities in fairness testing, to foster further advances in this area.

Figure 2 illustrates the structure of the paper, and Section 3 presents the detailed survey methodology.
